item.text: {"text":"Recent work supports representing histories with several evolving interests. [IMA/EMA (2024)](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/10400839/) retains existing intents, detects new ones, and removes inactive intents under memory constraints. [Multi-interest sequential recommendation with contrastive learning and temporal analysis (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.knosys.2024.112657) groups similar items into interest subgraphs, models short-term changes, and separates interests through contrastive learning. [D2MFRec (2025)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-025-31190-z) combines soft-clustered interest representations with a sequential representation through learned gates. These provide mechanisms for interest persistence, differentiation, and selective aggregation; they do not establish that an inactive interest represents a completed need.\n\nFor lightweight temporal modeling, [DSRec (September 2026 preprint)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.21548) separates stable historical preferences from short-term intent, using distinct state-space encoders and time-gap-modulated state evolution. A practical hypothesis suggested by these papers: maintain a small bank of causal interest states, softly route each interaction to a state, update it recurrently, and learn decay from elapsed time; combine state scores with a recent-history branch. Distinguishing recurring interests from incidental interactions or completed needs remains an inference problem without completion labels. Test decay, routing, and state diversity separately against SASRec using the fixed macro validation HR@10; interpret gains as predictive improvements, not evidence that the inferred states identify actual consumption completion."}
